profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the team building CSI, a prototype for Synchronized Software Development, and the internal developer-experience team integrating it into the company IDE workflow. A three-engineer backend pilot starts next week, and the two leads need to align on the interface and handoff between the synchronization backend and the IDE plugin. The agenda is to confirm what counts as a 'safe sync' during the pilot, what information will be passed as 'lock context' when overlapping edits are restricted, which concrete setup they mean by 'the pilot environment' for pre-rollout validation, and what is included in 'the pilot handoff' by Friday. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on responsibilities for the backend package, plugin wiring, validation, and rollout materials for the pilot.

members.name: Nina Rao
members.expertise: distributed systems, compiler-integrated tooling, collaboration backends
members.background: Nina leads the research-engineering team that built CSI and has spent the last year prototyping server-side propagation, compilation-error gating, and entity lock semantics on top of a Java language server.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to look stable without broadening scope, and is especially concerned about avoiding last-minute work on editor-specific interpretation, local-machine variability, or support expectations her team cannot absorb.
hidden_assumptions: For the pilot, 'safe sync' naturally means propagation only after the server can confirm a project-wide clean build on the sandbox branch.

When someone asks for 'lock context', the obvious thing to pass is the backend's existing symbol-scoped reservation information plus lock state, because UI rendering details belong on the client side.
The phrase 'the pilot environment' refers to the controlled staging setup her team uses for validation: pinned Java 17, the current language-server build, and the CSI backend in staging.
A 'pilot handoff' is the backend-to-integration-team handoff: service behavior is stable, interface details are shared, and sample payloads and notes are available for DevEx to finish wiring.
If something is not explicitly requested as new API surface, the integration team is expected to adapt to the current backend contract rather than assume additional fields or supporting artifacts.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: IDE plugins, developer workflows, internal tooling rollout
members.background: Leo owns the company's VS Code and JetBrains extensions plus onboarding tooling, and his team is responsible for making new engineering infrastructure usable inside everyday developer environments.
members.private_state: He wants to minimize ambiguity before exposing the pilot to engineers, and is worried that if the experience is confusing or inconsistent across workstations, his team will inherit the support burden during rollout.
hidden_assumptions: For a pilot, 'safe sync' means changes can appear as soon as the file a developer is editing is locally clean enough for work to continue, even if unrelated workspace issues still exist.

When people say 'lock context', they mean enough information for the IDE to present an actionable restriction without reverse-engineering backend internals, including file/range cues and a user-friendly owner label.

The phrase 'the pilot environment' refers to the standard managed laptop setup used by the three pilot engineers, since that is the environment that determines whether the integration is actually usable.
A 'pilot handoff' is the integration-to-pilot-user handoff: plugin build installed, behavior checked in normal dev setups, and a short note explaining what engineers will see.
If the backend team says a concept is already supported, it is reasonable to assume the interface exposes whatever details the plugin needs to make that support legible to end users.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the pilot should only auto-propagate on 'safe sync'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a change is safe to propagate only when the entire project compiles cleanly in the server-side sandbox validation flow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a change is safe to propagate when the edited file or immediate working set is locally error-free enough that the developer can continue without obvious disruption.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are endorsing the same cautious principle rather than debating whether gating should exist, so 'safe sync' feels like a shared technical term even though each imports the validation scope most natural to their role.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree Nina's team will pass the 'lock context' to the plugin.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this includes the current backend reservation data for the locked entity—symbol identity, lock state, and holder ID—leaving all IDE-facing interpretation and mapping to the plugin team.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this includes whatever context the plugin needs to directly explain the restriction to users, such as file location, affected range, readable owner information, and enough cues to display a clear banner or inline block.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'lock context' sounds helpfully comprehensive while remaining non-technical, so neither person feels a need to force a field-by-field breakdown; each assumes the omitted pieces are obviously part of the same package.

misalignment_points.topic: Which setup they mean by 'the pilot environment'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to validate behavior in 'the pilot environment' before rollout.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the isolated pilot staging setup with the sandbox branch, pinned toolchain versions, and the CSI backend running in staging.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the standard company-managed developer image on the three pilot engineers' laptops, including their IDE builds and extension settings.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both setups are legitimately associated with the upcoming pilot and commonly described with the same shorthand, so the term feels specific enough in context even though it points to different concrete environments.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to complete 'the pilot handoff' by Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 interprets 'the pilot handoff' as the backend team's handoff to DevEx: the synchronization service behavior is stable, the interface is shared, and test notes or sample payloads are available for integration.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 interprets 'the pilot handoff' as DevEx's handoff to the pilot engineers: the plugin is wired into the IDE, exercised in normal laptop setups, and accompanied by a short user-facing note.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase naturally suggests one continuous rollout milestone, and because both are discussing the same pilot and the same Friday date, each silently centers the handoff boundary that is operationally salient in their own workstream.
